# Time and Latency

::: {.callout-question}
Why is mean latency a dangerous lie in physical systems, and how does information age ($\Delta t$) dictate dynamic stopping distances ($d_{\text{stop}}$)?
:::

2. **Model Information Freshness ($\Delta t$):** Quantify how sensor data staleness degrades state estimation accuracy and physical safety margins.
3. **Analyze Tail Latency Distributions ($P_{99}, P_{99.9}$):** Measure why average benchmark metrics mask safety-critical operating system scheduling and memory bus contention stalls.

* **System:** Autonomous Mobile Warehouse Cart ($2.0\text{ m/s}$ nominal speed)
* **Incident:** Rover struck a descending steel roll-up door; front chassis crushed.
* **Telemetry Snapshot:** Mean vision pipeline inference latency was $28\text{ ms}$ ($35\text{ FPS}$). At $T+45.120\text{ s}$, a Linux background logging process triggered a major page fault and LPDDR5 memory bus stall; inference latency spiked to $240\text{ ms}$ ($P_{99.9}$ tail event).
* **Root Cause:** During the $240\text{ ms}$ compute freeze, the cart traveled $0.48\text{ meters}$ without evaluating obstacle distance; dynamic stopping distance exceeded remaining gap.
* **Architectural Flaw:** System was certified on mean benchmark latency rather than $P_{99}$ tails.
:::

| **What the MCU Permits (System 1)** | *Trusted · Deterministic · Real-Time MCU* | • Audits arrival age: $\Delta t_{\text{total}} = t_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{transduce}}$<br>• VETO if $\Delta t_{\text{total}}$ exceeds freshness wall ($\tau_{\text{wall}}$)<br>• Continuously computes: $d_{\text{stop}}(v, t_{\text{delay}})$ |

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
**The Sim-to-Real Delta:**
* **What Simulation Assumes:** Sensors deliver frames at perfect, unvarying $33.333\text{ ms}$ intervals; operating system thread scheduling has zero jitter; memory access is instantaneous.
* **What the Bench Measures:** DMA memory transfers compete with neural accelerator weight streaming; Linux kernel background daemons trigger 100+ ms latency tail spikes; clock skew between SoC and MCU induces artificial velocity estimation errors.
:::

## The World Sets the Clock: Physical Deadlines ($\tau_{\text{world}}$)

In classical digital computing, the clock is synthetic: a quartz crystal oscillates at a fixed frequency, and the processor steps through instructions at its own pace. If a computation takes longer than expected, the clock simply keeps ticking until the output is ready.

In physical systems, **the physical world sets the clock**. Every physical task defines a characteristic timescale—the **world deadline** ($\tau_{\text{world}}$)—within which a sensory observation must be converted into physical counter-force before the physical state diverges irreversibly:

| Latency Stage | Physical / Silicon Mechanism | Typical Latency Budget |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Transduction ($t_{\text{transduce}}$)** | Photodiode charge integration / IMU cantilever deflection | $5\text{--}15\text{ ms}$ (Vision) / $0.1\text{--}1.0\text{ ms}$ (IMU) |
| **2. DMA Ingestion ($t_{\text{dma}}$)** | Hardware DMA transfer across MIPI CSI-2 bus into shared DRAM buffer | $2\text{--}8\text{ ms}$ |
| **3. Perception ($t_{\text{perceive}}$)** | Preprocessing, spatial crop, and neural visual backbone encoding on NPU | $10\text{--}25\text{ ms}$ |
| **4. Policy Inference ($t_{\text{inference}}$)** | Forward pass of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) or diffusion planner | $20\text{--}60\text{ ms}$ |
| **5. Inter-Processor IPC ($t_{\text{ipc}}$)** | Serializing proposal chunk across shared SRAM mailbox to Cortex-M4 | $0.5\text{--}2.0\text{ ms}$ |
| **6. MCU Enforcement ($t_{\text{enforce}}$)** | Evaluating control barrier invariants, stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}}$, and clipping | $0.2\text{--}1.0\text{ ms}$ |
| **7. Actuator Rise Time ($t_{\text{actuator}}$)** | Motor coil electrical $L/R$ time constant to build magnetic flux and torque | $5\text{--}15\text{ ms}$ |

To engineer a dependable system, we deconstruct the total latency chain ($t_{\text{total}}$) into its discrete physical and computational stages:

1. **Transduction Delay ($t_{\text{transduce}}$):** The physical time required for photons to integrate in CMOS photodiode wells (exposure time: $5\text{--}15\text{ ms}$) or for capacitive micro-cantilevers in an IMU to deflect under acceleration ($0.1\text{--}1.0\text{ ms}$).
2. **DMA Ingestion Overhead ($t_{\text{dma}}$):** The time required for hardware Direct Memory Access engines to transfer raw sensor frames across deserializers and system buses into shared system memory ($2\text{--}8\text{ ms}$).
3. **Perception Tokenization ($t_{\text{perceive}}$):** Image preprocessing, spatial cropping, color space conversion, and neural visual backbone encoding on the edge NPU ($10\text{--}25\text{ ms}$).
4. **Policy Planning Inference ($t_{\text{inference}}$):** Forward inference of the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model or diffusion trajectory unrolling ($20\text{--}60\text{ ms}$).
5. **Inter-Processor Transport ($t_{\text{ipc}}$):** Serializing the trajectory proposal across the shared memory RPMSG ring buffer from the application processor (MPU) to the microcontroller (MCU) ($0.5\text{--}2.0\text{ ms}$).
6. **MCU Safety Enforcement ($t_{\text{enforce}}$):** Evaluating control barrier invariants, calculating dynamic stopping distances, and projecting candidate actions onto safe envelopes in FreeRTOS ($0.2\text{--}1.0\text{ ms}$).
7. **Actuator Electrical Rise Time ($t_{\text{actuator}}$):** The physical time required for motor coil inductance ($L/R$ electrical time constant) to build magnetic flux and produce physical mechanical torque ($5\text{--}15\text{ ms}$).

### The Closed-Loop Stability Criterion
A physical AI system maintains closed-loop stability if and only if the worst-case ($P_{99}$) cumulative latency plus a safety margin is strictly smaller than the world deadline:

$$t_{\text{total}}(P_{99}) + t_{\text{margin}} < \tau_{\text{world}}$$

If $t_{\text{total}}(P_{99}) \ge \tau_{\text{world}}$, the control loop becomes open-loop during latency spikes, leading to limit-cycle oscillations, mechanical shudder, or catastrophic collision.

---

## Information Freshness Decay ($\Delta t$) and the Freshness Wall

Sensor data decays the instant it is transduced. When an image frame arrives at a neural network, it does not describe the *current* state of the world; it describes where the world was at time $t_{\text{transduce}}$.

We define **Information Age** ($\Delta t$) at the instant of physical actuation as:

$$\Delta t = t_{\text{actuation}} - t_{\text{transduction}}$$

Consider an obstacle or target object moving in the workspace with characteristic velocity $v_{\text{target}}$. The spatial uncertainty ($\sigma_{\text{pos}}$) of the machine's belief expands linearly with information age:

$$\sigma_{\text{pos}}(t) = \sigma_0 + v_{\text{target}} \cdot \Delta t$$

Where $\sigma_0$ is the intrinsic sensor measurement noise.

$$\sigma_{\text{pos}}(t) = \sigma_0 + v_{\text{target}} \cdot \Delta t$$

Where $\sigma_0$ is the intrinsic sensor measurement noise.

| Operating Regime | Information Age $\Delta t$ | Physical State & Machine Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fresh Observation** | $\Delta t \ll \Delta t_{\text{wall}}$ | Spatial uncertainty is tightly bounded ($\sigma_{\text{pos}} < \text{clearance}$). Model proposals are physically valid and permitted. |
| **Degraded Freshness** | $\Delta t \to \Delta t_{\text{wall}}$ | Uncertainty approaches obstacle boundary. MCU safety enforcer derates commanded velocity. |
| **Beyond the Freshness Wall** | $\Delta t \ge \Delta t_{\text{wall}}$ | **State Drift Collapse:** Sensory evidence is stale. Proposals are invalidated and vetoed by the real-time reflex. |

As information age $\Delta t$ increases, spatial uncertainty expands until it intersects the task clearance threshold. Beyond this critical boundary—**the Freshness Wall** ($\Delta t_{\text{wall}}$)—the physical state has drifted so far that the learned proposal becomes invalid.

### The Capacity vs. Freshness Dilemma
A common mistake in physical AI system design is choosing a massive foundation model (e.g. 7-billion-parameter VLA) running at $2\text{ Hz}$ ($500\text{ ms}$ latency) over a compact, distilled model running at $50\text{ Hz}$ ($20\text{ ms}$ latency). 

Even if the 7B model possesses higher semantic reasoning capability, its predictions are based on $500\text{ ms}$ stale sensory evidence. In a dynamic physical environment, **a nimble model acting on fresh data consistently outperforms a massive model acting on stale history**.

---

## The Tail Latency Lie: Why $P_{99}$ Governs Physical Survival

In standard machine learning benchmarks, researchers report average throughput: *"Our vision-language model achieves 30 FPS (33.3 ms mean latency)."*

On embedded hardware, mean latency is irrelevant to physical safety. Operating system context switches, Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) bus contention, CPU cache misses, and garbage collection create heavy-tailed latency distributions.

| Latency Metric | Measured Value | Physical Manifestation on Hardware |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Mean Latency ($P_{50}$)** | $33.3\text{ ms}$ ($30\text{ FPS}$) | Standard inference throughput during uninterrupted execution. |
| **99th Percentile ($P_{99}$)** | $185.0\text{ ms}$ | Caused by Linux thread preemption and DMA memory bus contention. Occurs **1,800 times per hour** at $50\text{ Hz}$. |
| **Max Spike ($P_{99.9}$)** | $320.0\text{ ms}$ | Caused by page faults and Python GC. At $2.0\text{ m/s}$, the machine travels **$0.64\text{ meters}$ blind**. |

Consider the arithmetic of real-time control:

* A robotic arm running a control loop at $50\text{ Hz}$ executes **180,000 cycles every hour**.
* If the 99th percentile ($P_{99}$) latency spikes above the world deadline, the system experiences a control freeze **1,800 times per hour**—that is, once every two seconds.
* If a vehicle travels at $2.0\text{ m/s}$, a single $P_{99.9}$ latency spike of $250\text{ ms}$ causes the machine to travel **$0.50\text{ meters}$ completely open-loop** before evaluating its next decision.

In the physical world, survival is not governed by average speed; it is governed by the extreme tail of the latency distribution ($P_{99}, P_{99.9}, P_{\text{max}}$).

---

## Dynamic Stopping Distance Physics ($d_{\text{stop}}$)

The ultimate physical metric connecting computing latency to mechanical safety is the **Dynamic Stopping Distance** ($d_{\text{stop}}$): the total forward clearance required to bring a moving machine to a complete, safe stop before collision occurs.

$$d_{\text{stop}}(t) = v(t) \cdot t_{\text{delay}}(t) + \frac{v(t)^2}{2 \cdot a_{\text{max}}}$$

Where total reaction delay $t_{\text{delay}}$ incorporates the entire sensory-motor latency chain:

$$t_{\text{delay}}(t) = t_{\text{transduce}} + \Delta t_{\text{age}}(t) + t_{\text{comm}} + t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuator\_response}}$$

The stopping distance is composed of two distinct physical phases:

```text
DYNAMIC STOPPING DISTANCE COMPOSITION:
├───────────── Reaction Distance (v · t_delay) ─────────────┼─── Braking Distance (v² / 2a_max) ───┤
│                                                           │                                      │
▼ Obstacle Detected                                         ▼ Braking Begins                       ▼ Complete Stop
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

1. **The Reaction Phase ($v \cdot t_{\text{delay}}$):** The machine continues moving forward at unreduced velocity $v$ while photons integrate, neural networks compute, shared memory transmits, and MCU filters evaluate. Reaction distance scales **linearly with delay** and **linearly with velocity**.
2. **The Braking Phase ($\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}$):** The distance traversed while motor inverters apply maximum safe deceleration $a_{\text{max}}$ within friction limits ($\mu g$). Braking distance scales **quadratically with velocity**.

### Quantitative Systems Example
Consider a mobile manipulator moving at $v = 1.0\text{ m/s}$ with maximum safe braking deceleration $a_{\text{max}} = 2.0\text{ m/s}^2$:

* **Nominal Cycle ($t_{\text{delay}} = 30\text{ ms}$):**
  $$d_{\text{stop}} = (1.0 \cdot 0.030) + \frac{1.0^2}{2 \cdot 2.0} = 0.030\text{ m} + 0.250\text{ m} = \mathbf{0.280\text{ m}}$$
* **$P_{99}$ Tail Spike ($t_{\text{delay}} = 230\text{ ms}$):**
  $$d_{\text{stop}} = (1.0 \cdot 0.230) + \frac{1.0^2}{2 \cdot 2.0} = 0.230\text{ m} + 0.250\text{ m} = \mathbf{0.480\text{ m}}$$

A single latency tail spike increases the required physical stopping clearance by **$20\text{ cm}$ ($+71\%$)**. If the workspace obstacle margin is only $35\text{ cm}$, the nominal machine operates safely, but the machine experiencing $P_{99}$ tail spikes crashes violently.

## The Sensory-Motor Metrology Protocol and Hardware Instrumentation

To measure a Physical AI machine rigorously without introducing measurement artifacts:

```text
HARDWARE-TRIGGERED METROLOGY TOPOLOGY:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Optical / Magnetic Transduction Event               │
  │    (GPIO Output Pin Toggled on Sensor Arrival Interrupt)│
  └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                             │ Channel 1 (Transduce Pulse)
                             ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 2. Linux MPU VLA Inference Execution                   │
  │    (GPIO Toggled on RPMSG Buffer Write)                │
  └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                             │ Channel 2 (Inference Done)
                             ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 3. MCU Safety Filter Validation                        │
  │    (GPIO Toggled on PWM Register Write)                │
  └──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                             │ Channel 3 (PWM Output Active)
                             ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 4. Current Shunt Oscilloscope Probe                    │
  │    (Measures Physical Coil Current Rise dI/dt)         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. **Hardware-Triggered Instrumentation:** Use external oscilloscopes or logic analyzer GPIO toggles configured directly on hardware timer pins. Never use software print statements or user-space logging functions to measure real-time latency, as they perturb the scheduler.
2. **Microsecond Precision Clocks (PTP / IEEE 1588):** Synchronize the Linux application processor and real-time microcontroller to a shared hardware microsecond timebase.
3. **Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) Auditing:** Record at least 10,000 continuous execution cycles under simulated memory bus load (e.g. streaming background 4K video while executing neural inference). Plot the full empirical CDF to inspect $P_{50}, P_{90}, P_{99}$, and $P_{99.9}$ tails.

## Systems Fallacies and Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
### Common Engineering Fallacies
* **Fallacy 1:** *"A high camera frame rate (e.g. 60 FPS) guarantees low sensory latency."*  
  *Correction:* Frame rate measures pipeline throughput, not latency. A camera pipeline can deliver 60 FPS while buffering four frames internally in USB/DMA queues, adding $66.7\text{ ms}$ of stale information lag.
* **Fallacy 2:** *"Software timestamps generated with Python's `time.time()` or `std::chrono` accurately measure sensor arrival."*  
  *Correction:* Python timestamps record when the operating system scheduler dispatched the user thread, not when the physical photons hit the CMOS sensor.
* **Fallacy 3:** *"Average latency is a sufficient metric for certifying robotic safety."*  
  *Correction:* Average latency hides multi-hundred-millisecond tail spikes caused by memory bus contention and kernel interrupts. A system operating safely on average will regularly crash during tail events.
:::

```yaml

    dma_ingestion_max: 5.0

```
